Krispy Kreme Is Also Releasing Pokémon Cups

As part of the collection, Krispy Kreme is also debuting special-edition Pokémon cups available in five exclusive Pokémon designs. Each cup will be filled with 10 Original Glazed Gold Dots (aka mini doughnuts).
Krispy Kreme is Giving Out Free Doughnuts on Aug. 22

On Saturday, Aug. 22, Krispy Kreme customers who show up to their participating shops wearing Pokémon attire will score a free Original Glazed Doughnut. The single-use offer is available in shops and at the drive-thru.

title: The Osage Story ‘Little House on the Prairie’ Never Told — Until Now
summary: The Osage people’s story is finally incorporated into Little House on the Prairie thanks to the new movie. Here’s what to know.
story: In 1868, the Drum Creek Treaty pushed the Osage Nation from Kansas to present-day Oklahoma, then known as Indian Territory.

More than 150 years later, roughly 200 people gathered in Pawhuska, Oklahoma to revisit that history. Osage individuals, Netflix producers, actors and cultural and historical consultants filled the Osage Casino and Hotel for a screening of Episode 7 of the streamer’s new adaptation of “Little House on the Prairie,” which dramatizes the treaty’s signing.

Unlike the original stories, Netflix’s new eight-episode adaptation, which premiered July 9, highlights the story of the Osage people, whose land Laura Ingalls Wilder’s family illegally settled on in 1869, and were later pushed off of by the U.S. government.
The series primarily represents the Osage perspective through the fictional Mitchell family, whose storyline runs nearly parallel to the Ingalls family and provides an Indigenous lens on the story.
For the cast and crew who spent months trying to wrestle an erased history onto the screen, earning the Osage Nation’s approval was more important than that of any fan or critic.

The long-awaited verdict arrived when the credits rolled, and the Osage Nation principal chief approached actor Meegwun Fairbrother, who portrays farmer and father William Mitchell in the series. Fairbrother recalls the Chief telling him, “‘This is our stamp of approval. We like it,’” he tells TODAY.com.

Indigenous stories weren’t only left out in the original books and adaptation. In recent years, Wilder’s stories have also been criticized for including depictions of Indigenous people that reflect racial attitudes common among white settlers of the 19th century.

Production sought to strike a delicate balance: accurately portraying the Osage Nation’s fight to stay on their own land while also preserving the heart and “overall sensibility” of Wilder’s tales that drew readers to the stories in the first place, Robert Warrior, an Osage historical consultant and professor of American literature who worked with the show’s creators, tells TODAY.com.
Read on to learn more about the historical moment the series stepped into, and what it was like for the actors to depict Osage culture and history onscreen.
Bringing Osage History to Screen

When the Ingalls family made their famous journey to present-day Kansas, they arrived on land that wasn’t legally open to settlement. But Pa didn’t know that when he arrived, and neither did many of the settlers who showed up to claim land they had been told was available, Warrior explains.

Railroad companies also wanted access to the region, he says, and those economic interests often benefited from encouraging settlers to move into the area before legal questions about land rights were resolved.
The tensions in the region weren’t just between settlers and Indigenous people. Competing claims to land, political power and economic opportunity collided across the territory.

Facing displacement and hostility, Osage people were forced to make difficult decisions about survival, identity and their futures, the historian explains. Roughly 4,500 Osage people ultimately left their homeland and way of life in Kansas, and relocated to Oklahoma, what was then called Indian Territory, Warrior says.

But not all families made the choice to leave. About 19 Osage families chose to remain in Kansas, which is the historical basis for the Mitchell family storyline depicted in Netflix’s series. The few who stayed encountered intense discrimination: two heads of those families were killed by settlers, Warrior says, and nearly all eventually fled Kansas and joined the broader Osage community elsewhere.
Really, one of Warrior’s most important goals in consulting for the show was depicting that Osage people, like the Ingalls family, had their own ambitions, disagreements and family dynamics.
He sought to ensure they were afforded the same depth in the show’s storytelling as settler families.
“They’re not just 4,500 nameless people who are standing in the way of a railroad,” he says. “They are actual real people.”

Bringing complex Osage history, stories and culture to the screen entailed far more than just recreating historical events. Actors spent weeks studying cultural practices, learning the Osage language and building characters grounded in lived experience.
'Little House on the Prairie'

The True Story of Dr. George Tann, the Black Doctor Who Saved the Ingalls Family’s Lives in ‘Little House on the Prairie’See the Cast of the New ‘Little House on the Prairie’ Side-by-Side with the Original
The True Story of Dr. George Tann, the Black Doctor Who Saved the Ingalls Family’s Lives in ‘Little House on the Prairie’
See the Cast of the New ‘Little House on the Prairie’ Side-by-Side with the Original
Stars Meegwun Fairbrother and Alyssa Wapanatâhk Discuss the Roles

Wapanatâhk, who plays White Sun, William Mitchell’s wife, describes the Mitchell family as the “missing puzzle piece” in the “Little House” world, pointing to how Indigenous people existed in Wilder’s world but were largely absent from the franchise’s most famous books and onscreen incarnation.

For Wapanatâhk, the role was an effort of resisting shallow symbolism and insisting on lived detail: bearing the weight of an Osage blanket, understanding the historical dynamic between an Osage husband and wife and learning ordinary dialogue beyond the words in her script to build a “whole life” and “whole story” for White Sun, she tells TODAY.com.
For Wapanatâhk, who is of Cree descent, it was also important to portray an Indigenous marriage built on love, strength and partnership — a dynamic she says is largely underrepresented in media.

“A lot of times in TV and film with Indigenous characters, there’s always this sense of we’re just a part of the story to check the boxes,” she says. “We didn’t get that sense when we were reading this ... we got the sense that they were real people, a real family.”

Fairbrother, who is of Ojibwe descent, approached his role with a similar sense of responsibility. After both actors spent six weeks learning the Osage language, he embedded his learning not just into how he spoke, but how he moved. His goal, he says, was to portray a “4D character.”
“Somebody who laughs, somebody who cries, somebody who’s got conflict, but he’s doing his best to take care of his family and his community,” he says.

That commitment to multidimensionality shaped not only the effort put into the production experience, but also the version of Indigenous life portrayed to “Little House” audiences: complex people, loving families and perspectives that had always been a part of the frontier story, but rarely able to tell their stories in their own words.

title: Maria Canals-Barrera Raised Generations of Disney Channel Kids. This Is Her Story
summary: Maria Canals-Barrera raised a generation of Disney Channel stars and viewers. She speaks to TODAY.com about returning to “Camp Rock 3” and appearing in the series finale of “Wizards Beyond Waverly Place.”
story: Maria Canals-Barrera is a Disney Channel mom that viewers remember fondly.

For generations of tweens who spent their time repeatedly watching the “Camp Rock” movies or episodes of “Wizards of Waverly Place,” Canals-Barrera was a parental figure they trusted. Her roles as Connie Torres, the mom of Mitchie Torres played by Demi Lovato, and as Theresa Russo, the mom of Alex Russo played by Selena Gomez, were pivotal to the storylines and influential in the most subtle ways.

When Alex got scolded, fans took in the lessons Theresa was giving her. When Connie delivered good news to Mitchie, viewers experienced that same excitement. Canals-Barrera was an understated force that brought delight to many families’ screens.
“I feel very blessed to have been part of the two franchises that helped their diamonds, (Selena and Demi), not to mention all the other wonderful kids on our shows,” Canals-Barrera tells TODAY.com.

As time has gone by, Canals-Barrera has always kept “Camp Rock” and “Wizards” close to her heart. She’s back for “Camp Rock 3,” out now, and recently appeared in the finale of the “Wizards” spinoff, “Wizards Beyond Waverly Place.”
‘We Rock On’: Returning to the ‘Camp Rock’ Era
After appearing in 2008’s “Camp Rock” and its sequel, “Camp Rock 2: The Final Jam,” Canals-Barrera made her way back to the summer music camp to film the third movie.
Canals-Barrera noticed a resemblance between the original cast, that included Lovato and the Jonas Brothers, and the new Camp Rockers.
They brought that “same openness to show who they are,” she says. “Everybody had their own individual voice and style.”
The new cast includes Disney Channel stars Liamani and Malachi Barton, as well as Lumi Pollack, Hudson Stone and Casey Trotter.

The premise for “Camp Rock 3” differs a bit from the two previous iterations. This time, campers compete in a Final Jam to become the opening act for Connect 3, the band played by Joe, Kevin and Nick Jonas. Connie has now become director of the camp, guiding the new talent and taking charge.
There’s popular kids and misfits with a variety of artistic talents, new versions of old songs and references to the previous films — including *that* viral dance.

“I think the audience will be able to identify with at least one of the campers in their individual storylines,” Canals-Barrera says. The new cast, she says, has reimagined some of the classic tracks in “brilliant” ways. But the new music is still as danceable and of-the-times as ever. The Jonas Brothers also perform a new track, “Come On Over.”

Lovato also made her return to Camp Rock, but this time taking on an executive producer role. While it had been rumored she would make a surprise appearance, Lovato confirmed her cameo days before the release.
Canals-Barrera continues to feel connected to her on-screen daughter. Thinking of their initial time together, she says she loved working with Lovato.

“She was so easy to love, so easy to root for. Such a sweet, special person. She’s just this beam of light, that megawatt smile, that incredible vocal talent,” she says. “I loved doing my scenes with her.”
Her role as Connie was representative of something deeper: a hard-working parent, a thoughtful human and a leader.

“It wasn’t a thankless parent role, like, ‘Go to bed.’ It was life lessons. It was anchoring them in what the truth is and what matters and believing in themselves and that they are something special and different,” she says.
Her wisdom and love continues in “Camp Rock 3.”
Back to the Magic of ‘Wizards’
“Wizards of Waverly Place” was “like magic, no pun intended,” according to Canals-Barrera.

That spark fueled the show’s success, with an unmatched energy from Gomez’s Alex and a chemistry within the cast. The show’s comedy was witty and sharp, accentuated by Gomez’s delivery. Yet, one of the most memorable moments in the Emmy-winning show is when Theresa comforts Alex after a breakup.
“I know how much it hurts when your heart gets broken, but time will heal it,” Theresa begins, immediately adding, “On the bright side, we’re all really happy to see you have feelings.”

As Theresa continues to console Alex, humor comes through once again, saying the iconic line: “My parenting guide doesn’t have a chapter on what to do when your wizard daughter’s werewolf boyfriend has been in love with your son’s vampire girlfriend for the past 300 years.”

This experience of a parent feeling lost on how to help their kid or a child feeling like nobody understands, is universal. Viewers saw this moment and felt layers of emotions, like the warm hug that Theresa gives Alex to conclude their chat.
The nurturing energy extended beyond the characters she played. Canals-Barrera shares that she also gave motherly advice to the people she worked with, including Gomez.

“She asked me for relationship advice a couple of times during the show. And that was really honoring to me because I play her mom. I’m not her mom,” she says. “So when (Gomez) asked me a couple of times about marriage and stuff, that was really touching to me.”
As years went by and Gomez found love with Benny Blanco, marrying him in 2025, Canals-Barrera did not feel the need to share any more wisdom. “I think she figured it out,” Canals-Barrera says.
Canals-Barrera, who previously shared a video on social media confirming her attendance at Gomez’s wedding, called the event “so beautiful.”
Not only was “Wizards of Waverly Place” a Disney Channel hit, it also received critical acclaim, winning two Emmys for outstanding children’s program in 2009 and 2012.
Canals-Barrera says the show’s success is “because we really loved each other and the Russos really had each other’s back ... That real commitment and that real love makes sitcoms unforgettable.”
Representation On Screen, Motherhood Off Screen
Canals-Barrera has always celebrated her Latin roots. When looking for roles, her focus was to show her many layers.

“I’m American and I have this Cuban heritage ... with all the richness. To me, it was a plus,” she says. “And then you get to Hollywood, and Hollywood puts you in these boxes. I’m like, wait a minute. I’m everything. I’m not just one thing. Let me be everything that I am.”

As Canals-Barrera’s made it to Disney, she says, the “Camp Rock” and “Wizards” castings were organic and based on talent. She explains that there weren’t conversations specifying her characters’ ethnicities.

“It just was,” Canals-Barrera says about her roles, as well as Gomez and Lovato’s, who are of Latino descent. “What I love about it is that these lovely ladies were chosen because of their skill, because of their talent and their uniqueness. And the fact that they’re also of Latino heritage is just icing on the cake.”
She praises Lovato for her “incredible skills,” adding, “She got the part because she can sing like nobody’s business. She’s an amazing, funny and incredible actress.”
Gomez, she says, “is a born talent.” “She was on set knowing her lines, completely emotionally prepared and a singer to boot.”

Playing a mom to teenagers before becoming a mother herself gave Canals-Barrera a glimpse at what could be in her future. However, she quips, “Nothing prepares you for the teen years ... not even Alex Russo.”

The actor became a mom to daughters Bridget and Madeleine while actively working. Married to husband David Barrera since 1999, Canals-Barrera put the idea of becoming a mother to the side because of her career.
But at the age of 36 and a wake-up call from her sister, she and her husband felt ready.

“We had been prepared, emotionally, spiritually. We were married for years already and we wanted to (become parents),” she says, adding, “It was my sister who said, ‘Hello, you don’t have all the time in the world.’”
She recalls thinking “anything can happen in this business” and began to plan a family. “Everything worked out beautifully.”

With her daughters, now 23 and 21, and career on the path that she dreamed of, Canals-Barrera combined her two passions. She’s been able to bring her daughters along for the ride, most recently to the set of “Camp Rock 3.”
With fond memories of her Disney days of past and present, the actor repeatedly expresses her appreciation for her fans.
“I’m just in a state of gratitude, honestly, for having been able to play these awesome roles and be part of two amazing franchises,” she says.

title: Mariska Hargitay Wants Jalen Brunson to Make an ‘SVU’ Cameo
summary: Mariska Hargitay is manifesting the next “Law & Order: Special Victims Unit” guest star.
story: Mariska Hargitay is manifesting the next “Law & Order: Special Victims Unit” guest star.

The actor, who’s preparing to host the Primetime Emmy Awards this September, has had a packed schedule. After wrapping up a weekslong run on Broadway this summer in the starring role of the show “Every Brilliant Thing,” Hargitay has jumped into filming another season of “SVU.” And she’s got her sights set on a cameo from none other than New York Knicks captain Jalen Brunson.

Hargitay, a die-hard Knicks fan who was famously spotted at a number of games during the team’s championship run, hinted at a potential collaboration with the NBA champ Aug. 13, while discussing her latest projects live on TODAY. She took the opportunity to put a big wish into the universe.
“And I’m hoping that we might — don’t tell anyone, but — see (Brunson) on ‘SVU,’” she told TODAY host Savannah Guthrie.
“I won’t tell anyone,” Savannah promised.

Earlier this summer, the actor was spotted sitting courtside next to Taylor Swift at Game 4 of the NBA Finals. Hargitay even changed outfits mid-game since she rushed over to attend the game after wrapping up a Broadway performance.

She has attended many of the team’s games and has even found ways to incorporate her love of the Knicks into her performances.  For instance, during a June performance of “Every Brilliant Thing,” the actor brought a Knicks jersey on stage.

During their chat, Savannah remarked to Hargitay that “everything you’re touching is turning to gold right now, including Jalen Brunson and the Knicks,” referencing the team’s NBA finals win in June, ending a 53-year championship drought.
“That is all super surreal still, all of that, but I’m really thrilled,” Hargitay replied.
Savannah also joked that Hargitay should continue to reveal more tea and hopefully, the actor’s wishes will materialize.
“We’ll have to manifest a few more,” Savannah said. “Let’s cook up some more stuff.”

Hargitay has actually managed to bring up the Knicks and her friendship with Brunson on several occasions. While appearing on TODAY with Jenna & Sheinelle in June, Hargitay referred to Brunson as a “friend” and said he’s “my inspiration.”
“He is so singular and magnificent. He’s a magnificent human,” she said.
When guest co-host Savannah suggested that Brunson should attend Hargitay’s Broadway show, the actor said, “Oh, he told me he’s coming!”
The ‘SVU’ star also sat down with Hoda Kotb for a June episode of her “Making Space” podcast in June and applauded the athlete and his teammates for their performance in the NBA Finals.
“Here, the Knicks have had this profound effect on the city and provided hope, but also the ability to dig deep and all of the things that we learn (like) never give up,” she said.
The actor spoke fondly of Brunson and praised “what he’s done and what he’s taught us and children.”
“So he’s teaching you? Jalen Brunson is teaching you?” Kotb asked.
“Every day,” Hargitay replied.

title: Canada races to avoid new U.S. tariffs of up to 50%
summary: The duties would hit a wide swath of goods, including hockey sticks, building materials, clothing and dairy products.
story: The Canadian government is racing to negotiate a deal with the Trump administration in order to avoid a fresh wave of U.S. tariffs set to hit many of its exports to the United States starting on Wednesday.
However, after weeks of meetings, the prospects for a deal remained uncertain Monday, and Canadian broadcaster CBC reported that the two countries were at an impasse.
Speaking to reporters, Prime Minister Mark Carney described the talks as “very delicate and intense.” He also said he planned to speak with Trump before the deadline.

The new tariffs, if implemented, would hit about $20 billion worth of Canadian products imported to the U.S., including hockey sticks, some clothing, wines, some dairy products and certain building materials such as cement and plywood. Energy products, potash, fish and critical minerals are excluded from the duties.
In 2025, Canada ranked as the third-largest source of imports for the U.S., according to Census Bureau data, with more than $380 billion worth of goods crossing the border into the U.S. last year.

The White House has said the tariffs are in response to Canada’s “discriminatory treatment of American products” and that it’s “leveling the playing field for crucial American exports — cars, alcohol, and dairy.”

It plans to implement the duties under Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, a 96-year-old law that authorizes the president to hit any foreign country that discriminates against U.S. commerce with tariffs of up to 50%.
No president has ever invoked Section 338 before, and legal challenges are all but certain to be filed against the tariffs.

Nonetheless, importers could pass the new tariffs down to consumers — putting more pressure on Americans who are already navigating higher costs. Consumer prices have jumped 3.4% over the last year, up from 2.4% right before the Iran war.
Tariffs currently cost the average American household around $1,100 annually, Yale’s Budget Lab estimates.
A trade cold war gets hot

For more than a year, the U.S. and Canada have engaged in a trade tit for tat. The U.S. put in place global tariffs on imports including steel, aluminum and autos last year — as well as IEEPA tariffs on Canada over alleged fentanyl trafficking at the northern border.

Canada denied that its border was a significant source of fentanyl smuggling into the U.S. and retaliated with tariffs of its own on American products. Now, U.S. officials say these new tariffs are payback for Canada’s retaliation.

“The policy basis for [Wednesday’s] duties are related to measures that Canada took against the United States,” U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said last week. “I’ve got two countries in the world that have retaliated against the United States for trade measures: the People’s Republic of China and Canada,” said Greer. “That’s not the kind of company you really want to be running in.”

Carney, in a statement, called the threatened duties “the latest in a series of unilateral U.S. trade actions” that have been in “direct violation” of the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement — a trade deal Trump signed during his first term.

title: Kushner and Netanyahu agree U.S. general should oversee Hamas ‘demilitarization,’ source says
summary: The agreement came during an hourslong meeting, which followed rare talks between the leader of Hamas, Kushner and other members of Trump’s Board of Peace.
story: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and President Donald Trump’s son-in-law and envoy Jared Kushner on Monday agreed that the Gaza Strip’s “demilitarization” should start with a Hamas weapons handover supervised by an American military general, according to a senior Israeli official.

The agreement came during an hourslong meeting, which followed rare talks between the leader of Hamas, Kushner and other members of Trump’s Board of Peace — part of a renewed push to revive a Gaza peace plan endorsed by Trump and Hamas but rejected by Israel.
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the details of the meeting provided by the senior Israeli official.

U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee and former British Prime Minister Tony Blair joined Netanyahu and Kushner. A board official told NBC News this weekend that former European Parliament lawmaker Nickolay Mladenov, now Trump’s Board of Peace envoy for Gaza, was also expected to attend.
Add to Google
Add to Google

Netanyahu and Kushner also agreed that no reconstruction of Gaza should begin before Hamas is disarmed and that “necessary measures” should be taken to “address sanitation and environmental concerns,” the official added.
Netanyahu “made it clear” that the Israel Defense Forces will not redeploy but that it would “continue to thwart” threats to its forces and the residents of Israel, the official said.

In a statement, Netanyahu’s office did not confirm the details given by the Israeli official, instead saying only that the meeting had agreed to establish two working groups: one focusing on disarmament and demilitarization and the other centering on sanitation, clean water and other public health issues “for the people of Gaza and which also impact the people of Israel.”
Both Israel and the Board of Peace agree that the disarmament and demilitarization piece “should be prompt and completed before any reconstruction happens in Gaza,” the prime minister’s office said.

The U.S. and Israel have shown rare public divisions over the road map for the future of the Palestinian enclave, as well as the Israeli government’s approach to a mounting crisis in the occupied West Bank.

The renewed diplomatic effort comes as Netanyahu faces growing domestic pressure ahead of Israeli elections in October, including from the far-right faction upon which his fragile coalition government relies.

Netanyahu earlier this month rejected Trump’s 15-point plan, which would require Hamas’ disarmament and Israel’s withdrawal from Gaza, with the Israeli leader vowing that there would be no military pullout until Hamas is “genuinely disarmed.”

title: Trump orders military to ‘substantially reduce’ joint exercises with South Korea
summary: The president said he has directed the Pentagon to scale down the exercises, citing South Korea’s refusal to join the war in Iran and his “very good” relationship with North Korea’s Kim Jong Un.
story: President Donald Trump said Sunday that he has directed the Defense Department to scale down joint military exercises with South Korea, citing the U.S. ally’s refusal to join the war in Iran and his “very good” relationship with North Korea’s Kim Jong Un.

Trump said the large, annual military drills sent a “signal that is totally inappropriate and hostile” to North Korea, a nuclear-armed state with which the U.S. has no formal diplomatic ties but which Trump says has been “unthreatening and respectful” as long as he has been president.

“Based on the fact that it is too late to cancel, I have instructed Secretary of War, Pete Hegseth, to substantially reduce the Joint Military Exercises!” Trump wrote on social media. His announcement came just hours before the drills were set to start.
Kim Jong Un rides a tank driven by his teenage daughter
Trump also mentioned South Korea’s refusal to join the Iran war.

“While somewhat unrelated (?), I recently asked the President of South Korea if they would like to join us in the Denuclearization of the Islamic Republic of Iran, and they said, ‘No thanks!’” Trump wrote.

It was not immediately clear what a scaled-down version of the training would look like. The South Korean defense ministry said Monday that the drills, known as Ulchi Freedom Shield and scheduled to last until Aug. 27, were “proceeding as planned.”

In a statement on Monday, the office of South Korean President Lee Jae Myung said the U.S. and South Korea had “maintained close coordination” on joint exercises and training and would continue to do so.

Like Trump, Lee has expressed support for the resumption of talks with North Korea, which remains technically at war with South Korea after the Korean War ended in 1953 with an armistice rather than a peace treaty.

The government “hopes that the friendly relationship between the leaders of the United States and North Korea will lead to meaningful U.S.-North Korea dialogue, thereby opening discussions aimed at advancing peace and stability on the Korean Peninsula,” Lee’s office said. “To this end, the government will make the necessary diplomatic efforts as a ‘pace-setter,’ in close coordination with the United States.”

Lee’s office said the South Korean government had “actively participated” in international talks aimed at reaching a ceasefire in Iran and restoring freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz and that it was also in close consultation with the U.S. “regarding practical and military contributions.”

According to U.S. Forces Korea, the military exercises are meant to build understanding among several agencies to ensure “their ability to fortify the combined defense posture and enhance Alliance response capabilities against a spectrum of security threats.” North Korea routinely criticizes the annual drills as a “war rehearsal,” which the U.S. and its allies deny, and threatens to retaliate.
South Korea’s embassy in Washington and U.S. Forces Korea did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Trump’s call to curtail the exercises was criticized by lawmakers such as Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., who said they help the U.S. better defend South Korea against the North.
“Hollowing out these joint exercises is shortsighted and a mistake,” he said in a post on X.
The exercises “are essential for military forces to be ready and capable of doing their jobs,” said Leif-Eric Easley, professor of international studies at Ewha Womans University in Seoul.

“Scaling them back can damage alliance coordination, slow the process of South Korea taking on greater responsibility for its own defense, and weaken deterrence against possible conflicts in Asia,” he said in emailed comments.

It is also unlikely to win Trump a meeting with Kim, who has shown no interest in resuming talks after their earlier diplomatic efforts collapsed in 2019. Since then, Kim has advanced his nuclear and missile programs and built ties with Russia by providing troops and weapons for its war on Ukraine.

“Trump’s recent social media posts about Kim Jong Un suggest a willingness to re-engage, but North Korea is busy profiting from Russia’s war against Ukraine while modernizing its own military,” Easley said.
Trump’s announcement comes days after North Korea launched a ballistic missile toward the sea, conducting weapons testing in possible protest of the upcoming U.S.-South Korea military drills.

It also comes a day after the U.S. pulled its last aircraft carrier in Asia, as the USS George Washington was sent to replace the USS Abraham Lincoln — which has drawn scrutiny over conditions on board — in the Persian Gulf.

title: Woman leaps from 11th-floor ledge into firefighter’s arms as Berlin high-rise burns
summary: As a furious blaze raged inside a high-rise apartment building in Berlin, one woman was rescued by scaling the building’s exterior and taking a terrifying leap more than two stories down to safety.
story: As a furious blaze raged inside a high-rise apartment building in Berlin, one woman was rescued by scaling the building’s exterior and taking a terrifying leap more than two stories down to safety.
The fire erupted in an 18-story residential high-rise building in the German capital’s Friedrichshain neighborhood around 6:30 a.m. Friday, The Associated Press reported.

The blaze started in an apartment on the 11th floor and spread to the apartment above it, with flames shooting from several windows and thick, black smoke pluming from the building, Berlin police said.

The dramatic rescue, captured on video, shows a woman in sweatpants scaling the exterior of an 11th-floor apartment, edging perilously along a window ledge as giant orange flames and black smoke billow from the apartment beside her.
Two floors below her outside, a firefighter is seen in the basket of a turntable ladder used for elevated rescues.

She spends several tense minutes trying to climb down to the apartment below, but can’t find footing. Finally, she lets go of the ledge and takes a heart-stopping leap, falling into a rescue basket held by the firefighter, who catches her.

Police said the woman, who was not identified, jumped roughly two floors down into the basket and was safely caught. She sustained minor injuries and was taken to a hospital for treatment, police said.

In total, the fire affected 115 people. Twenty-five were rescued or brought to safety via fire-escape hoods on the stairwell and a turntable ladder, police said. Thirteen people suffered minor injuries and received emergency medical treatment, with some transported to nearby hospitals for further care.
Authorities described the response as “especially strenuous and requiring a significant number of personnel” given the number of people affected and the scale of the fire.
Eighteen fire engines, two aerial ladder trucks, nine ambulances and more were deployed to quell the blaze and carry out rescues. The cause of the fire is not yet known.

title: Jason Arday, ex-Cambridge professor accused of plagiarism, found dead a week after resigning
summary: Former Cambridge professor Jason Arday was found dead at his London home on Friday, one week after he resigned from his position after accusations of plagiarism.
story: A former Cambridge professor was found dead at his London home on Friday, one week after he resigned from his position at the esteemed university following accusations of plagiarism.
Jason Arday, 41, became the youngest Black professor at Cambridge when he was hired as a professor of sociology of education in 2023.

London’s Metropolitan Police force said it responded to a report of a man found unresponsive inside a property on Friday and that the man was pronounced dead at the scene, without naming Arday. Authorities said the death is being treated as “unexpected, but is not believed to be suspicious.”

“We are desperately saddened to hear this tragic news. Our heartfelt sympathies go to Jason Arday’s family and friends at this incredibly difficult time,” University of Cambridge Vice-Chancellor Deborah Prentice said Friday.

Arday was known for his neurodivergence; he had said he was diagnosed with autism as a child and was unable to speak until the age of 11. He went on to forge a path in academia as a scholar of race, inequality and education.
Arday had resigned on Aug. 5 following scrutiny over alleged plagiarism in his academic work and questions about his accomplishments.

Last month, questions regarding his qualifications were raised publicly by Nathan Cofnas, a former Cambridge philosophy researcher who left the institution after critiquing diversity, equity and inclusion programs.

The Times of London had subsequently published an analysis of Arday’s 2015 Ph.D. thesis highlighting passages that it said were “identical or near-identical” to an earlier paper written by another researcher.
In the weeks since, British media outlets led intense and prolonged scrutiny of Arday’s work, also interrogating a history of claims about his childhood and personal life.

A statement from Arday’s family said he was “a gentle man and who always wanted to see the best in everyone,” condemning critics who they said “would leave no stone unturned in their quest to undermine him.”
Cambridge professor Simon Baron-Cohen, director of the university’s Autism Research Centre, told the BBC he was in touch with Arday hours before his death.

He said Arday “was being subjected to relentless scrutiny, including ridicule, discrediting absolutely every detail of his life,” adding that he “wasn’t coping with the loss of his career, the loss of his reputation, and he felt he couldn’t go on.”

Baron-Cohen said that Arday had believed “there was a racist playbook to discredit Black academics in universities, and that they used accusations of plagiarism to try and bring down Black academics,” adding that Arday referred to former Harvard President Claudine Gay, who resigned two years ago while facing plagiarism allegations and criticism over her comments on antisemitism.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Saturday that the death was “a tragedy on so many levels,” adding that “it’s not a moment for any rushing to judgment. It’s a moment for reflection, I would say.”

Other figures were more vocal in questioning his treatment by the media. London Mayor Sadiq Khan said on X that Arday had faced “an unacceptable public hounding and campaign of abuse” and that he “was the victim of a pernicious public shaming that other people in his position simply wouldn’t have faced.”

Hacked Off, a campaign group that supports regulation of the media, called for an “inquiry into the culture and behaviour of the British press” following the death, saying scrutiny “went far beyond any limited public interest considerations around academic standards.”
While Cambridge initially defended Arday, on Aug. 5 it opened an investigation “following new information about Professor Arday’s qualifications and honorary appointments.”

In his resignation statement last week, Arday described his tenure as “the privilege of my life to teach my students,” but conceded “the years since my appointment have also been marked by an unrelenting level of public scrutiny and personal attack.”

“While criticism is an inevitable part of academic life, what I have experienced has gone far beyond scholarly disagreement. The relentless accusations, speculation and public commentary have taken a profound toll on me and on those I love,” he continued.

In a statement Thursday, Cambridge’s Prentice shared an update on the inquiry into Arday, saying the university would investigate the circumstances around his appointment by the Faculty of Education in 2022 and his time at Cambridge.

She also said she asked the university council’s deputy chair and council’s audit committee to establish terms for an independent review of all university processes that will take place alongside the probe into Arday.
In his resignation announcement, Arday said he reached a point where the “personal cost becomes too great.”

“For my own wellbeing, for my family, and for those who have stood by me throughout this difficult period, I have concluded that the only way to bring this chapter to an end is to step away,” he said.

Arday’s memoir, “Great and Unfortunate Things,” was released earlier this week in the U.S., giving an account of his childhood — from being diagnosed with autism and developmental delays at the age of 3 — to speaking by the age of 11 and reading and writing by the age of 18.

“Without romanticizing the struggle, this is a story of determination against seemingly insurmountable odds — and of a family and a small group of believers whose compassion helped him see what is possible,” a description for the book by publisher Simon & Schuster said.

title: Magnitude-7.7 quake hits off coast of Indonesia, killing at least 47
summary: A magnitude-7.7 earthquake hit off the coast of Indonesia in the eastern Flores region, the United States Geological Survey reported on Friday.
story: A magnitude-7.7 earthquake hit off the coast of Indonesia in the eastern Flores region, the United States Geological Survey reported on Friday.
The epicenter was 42 miles north-northwest of the city of Ende in East Nusa Tenggara province.
At least 47 people have been killed, the ​National Disaster Management Agency said Saturday.
Rescue teams have yet to reach Nagekeo, the region ‌closest to the epicenter, after landslides blocked roads and disrupted communications, officials said.

“The quake was massive, the shock was so strong,” Nona, a 51-year-old resident of Talibura, a village in East Nusa Tenggara, told Reuters. “There were 13 of us inside the house and we all ran to save ourselves.”

Earlier, ​rescuers in the port town of Maumere found 20 dead, six injured and two trapped under the rubble, ⁠said Fathur Rahman, head of the city’s rescue agency. Maumere is the main town in Sikka Regency on Flores Island in the east of ​Indonesia’s vast archipelago.
Residents remain trapped in several buildings in earthquake-affected areas, with reports of landslides blocking several roads.

Preliminary data ​showed 157 homes were heavily damaged, 41 moderately damaged and 148 lightly damaged. Damage was also reported at 87 schools, 18 health facilities, five places of worship and six office ‌buildings, along ⁠with other infrastructure.
The quake was felt across much of Flores Island, with reports indicating heavy damage.
Yohanna Embu, a resident of Sikka Regency, said a number of buildings were damaged by the strong shaking and panicked people ran to higher ground.
“Many buildings here were damaged. ... I saw that the waiting room at the port terminal in Maumere had collapsed,” she said.

Indonesian authorities initially issued a tsunami warning for parts of East Nusa Tenggara, West Nusa Tenggara, South Sulawesi and Southeast Sulawesi provinces, and urged residents to stay away from beaches and riverbanks, and residents on the coastline to move to higher ground. The agency located the shallow undersea quake near Flores Island.
The initial quake was followed by two aftershocks.

Students at St. Peter Major Seminary in Sikka who were attending morning Mass fled in panic when the roof of an assembly hall collapsed, said the Rev. Guidelbertus Tanga, rector of the seminary, which is known locally as Ritapiret Seminary on the predominantly Catholic island of Flores.
“Our students and nuns ran out in panic beneath a collapsing roof,” Tanga said, “At least one priest suffered a broken leg after jumping from the second floor of a building during the quake.”
Separately, Australia’s tsunami warning center said the undersea earthquake will have “no tsunami threat to the Australian mainland, islands or territories.”

Indonesia, a vast archipelago of more than 17,000 islands, is prone to earthquakes and volcanic activity because of its location on the “Ring of Fire,” an arc of volcanoes and fault lines in the Pacific Basin.
In December 1992, a magnitude-7 earthquake caused a tsunami that killed about 2,500 people on the southeastern island of Flores, part of a group of islands in the eastern half of Indonesia.
The latest quake comes after a 7.4-magnitude earthquake rocked western Colombia on Monday, causing widespread damage.
In June, deadly back-to-back earthquakes, with magnitudes of 7.2 and 7.5, killed more than 6,000 people in Venezuela, according to government figures.

title: Iran rejects ‘delusions’ after Trump says he wants the Strait of Hormuz to be a U.S. territory
summary: Iran called on the U.S. to “accept the reality of defeat” after President Donald Trump said he would declare the Strait of Hormuz a “territory” of the U.S.
story: TEHRAN, Iran — A defiant Iran called on the U.S. to “accept the reality of defeat and stop indulging in delusions” after President Donald Trump suggested that he would soon declare the Strait of Hormuz a “territory of the United States.”

The crucial waterway that handled one-fifth of the world’s oil before the war “cannot be seized with a tweet, nor with an aircraft carrier, nor by issuing an order, nor through an election speech,” Iran’s Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said in a post on X early Saturday.

“This strait will only be opened and closed under Iran’s command, and as long as you do not accept the reality of defeat and stop indulging in delusions, Iran will continue to enforce the blockade,” he added.

With oil tanker traffic through the strategic strait at a trickle and peace talks between the U.S. and Iran at an impasse, there are few signs that the war, launched on Feb. 28, is close to being over.

A 60-day negotiating period intended to hammer out a deal to end the conflict, set when Trump and Tehran signed a memorandum of understanding in mid-June, ends Monday with few direct negotiations having taken place.

Speaking Friday at a police academy in Nassau County, New York, Trump said Iran was being “very badly defeated,” and once victory was secured, “pretty soon, I’ll be declaring the Hormuz Strait a territory of the United States.”

Urging Americans to accept slightly higher gasoline prices, he told the crowd of law enforcement officers that “a tiny little bit more” at the pump was worth the cost of ensuring “a very ⁠evil country” could not have a nuclear weapon, one of his stated reasons for the war.

Global oil and gas markets have calmed since prices spiked at the start of the war, but prices are still significantly higher than before the conflict, and they rose again early Friday. Crude oil futures rose $1 a barrel Friday, while benchmark Brent futures were on track for a weekly rise of 6.0%, Reuters reported Saturday.
Which economy would benefit the most from end of U.S.-Iran war?

Traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remains a trickle of the 130 to 140 vessels that typically traverse it during peacetime. Only two vessels passed through the strait Friday, with no crude oil shipments visible, according to analysis from ship-tracking firm Kpler.
While some ships have turned their transponders off and risked crossing undetected, Iran continues to fire on ships attempting to transit despite the U.S. blockade of the Islamic Republic’s ports.

A ​bulk carrier was struck in the hull by an unknown projectile in the Strait of Hormuz on Friday, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Center ‌said Saturday. The organization run by the British navy that helps protect commercial shipping in high-risk areas added that the crew was safe, although no damage assessment had ⁠been reported and the environmental impact was unknown.

Vice President JD Vance, who has been tasked with leading negotiations to end the war, told Fox News on Thursday that the No. 1 goal was to “keep oil and gas cheap for Americans all over our country.” He added that “obviously goal No. 2 is ensure that Iran never gets a nuclear weapon.” Tehran has repeatedly insisted it has no desire to develop one.

Trump and his team have offered various reasons for the conflict, initially saying they wanted to support mass antigovernment protests, before prioritizing a desire to end Iran’s nuclear program and topple the hard-line Islamic regime.
In an interview with Iran’s Shahrara News published Friday, the country’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said there were “no negotiations currently taking place between Tehran and Washington.”

Qatar and Pakistan, as mediators, were exchanging messages and remained in contact with Iran, “but this does not at all constitute negotiations,” he said. “No decision has yet been taken to resume talks with America.”
Amin Khodadadi reported from Tehran and Henry Austin from London.

title: ‘Revenge is inevitable’: Iran ramps up propaganda war with violent billboards
summary: Anti-U.S. messaging has intensified since the death of Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, with artificial intelligence playing a major role.
story: The billboards are state-sponsored, plastered across Iran’s capital and far from subtle. One features an image of President Donald Trump lying in a casket; another shows the White House on fire; a third is a parody of the American flag with skulls in place of the stars and bombs dropping from the stripes.

Alongside ads for a multitude of products such as cars and shampoo, the giant billboards have become familiar sights to the people of Tehran in recent years. But since the country’s supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, was killed in an airstrike on the first day of the war launched by the United States and Israel, the messaging has become bolder and the tone more violent during the almost six-month conflict.

title: In an apparent shift, Vance says lowering oil prices is ‘goal No. 1’ of Iran war
summary: Keeping gas prices low is now the United States’ “goal No.
story: Keeping gas prices low is now the United States’ “goal No. 1” in the Iran war, Vice President JD Vance has said, as Washington threatened an indefinite naval blockade and signaled it would soon intensify economic pressure on Tehran.
The comments appeared to be the latest shift in the public rationale for the conflict, with Vance ranking Iran’s nuclear ambitions second.

The vice president’s remarks came as the Trump administration embraced a long-term effort to inflict more damage on the Islamic Republic, despite growing signs of strain on American forces and domestic pressure ahead of the midterm elections.

President Donald Trump has suggested a shift away from military force in favor of “low-keying it” with economic pressure. That followed a deadly cycle of tit-for-tat exchanges that produced no clear resolution and depleted U.S. reserves of missile interceptors.
Add to Google
Add to Google

Oil and gas prices spiked worldwide after the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28. Markets have since calmed since that early peak, but prices are still significantly higher than before the conflict and rose again early Friday after the most recent remarks from Vance and others.

“I know that oil is down today and it’s way down from the highs in the early days of the conflict,” Vance told Fox News on Thursday, before the latest uptick. “That’s goal No. 1 — keep oil and gas cheap for Americans all over our country.”
He added that “obviously goal No. 2 is ensure that Iran never gets a nuclear weapon.” Tehran insists it has no desire to develop one.

Trump and his team have offered various reasons for conflict with Iran, initially saying they wanted to support mass anti-government protests, before prioritizing a desire to defang Iran’s nuclear program and even topple the regime.

title: ‘Tinderbox’ Britain bans disposable barbecues, sends nationwide fire alerts as Europe battles blazes
summary: LONDON — The U.K. imposed a temporary ban on the sale of disposable barbecues and sent a nationwide alert warning of a “very high risk of wildfires” as European countries battle to keep blazes under control.
story: LONDON — The U.K. imposed a temporary ban on the sale of disposable barbecues and sent a nationwide alert warning of a “very high risk of wildfires” as European countries battle to keep blazes under control.

Authorities are bracing for the prospect of fires breaking out in the days ahead, with drought conditions across much of Britain and a prolonged heat wave this week bringing temperatures in excess of 38 degrees Celsius (100 degrees Fahrenheit).

“Britain is a tinderbox right now,” Prime Minister Andy Burnham warned on Friday as he visited the scene of a fire in Stourbridge, in the West Midlands region, that destroyed 19 homes. “I’ve never seen scenes like this in Britain,” he added.

Wildfires are not typically a major threat in Britain, usually known for a temperate maritime climate and frequent wet weather, even in the summertime. The U.K. does not have any firefighting planes, a common sight in many other countries, but Burnham said he would seek to commission some in an effort to “face up” to the “changing climate.”
“Farmers are watching crops fail and firefighters have faced hundreds of wildfires in a matter of weeks,” he added in a video shared on X. “This is what climate change looks like here and now.”
Many of England’s rolling green fields are currently a sea of brown, dried-out grass, with firefighters and officials fearing any spark could lead to catastrophe.
One Stourbridge resident said that trees were “exploding” in the conditions as the fire spread.
“We just grabbed everything and left,” Paul Nash, whose garden was damaged, told Reuters.
Burnham also announced a temporary ban on the sale of popular disposable barbecues.

“Retailers have been informed that disposable barbecues must be removed from sale immediately. The temporary measure will remain under review but will stay in place while the heightened wildfire risk continues,” the U.K. government said in a statement.

Emergency alerts were sent to phones across England and Wales nationwide on Friday, warning: “Residents, landowners and visitors should not undertake any activity that could start a fire, including disposable barbeques, firepits, garden incinerators or fireworks.
“Even a small flame can rapidly develop into a major wildfire placing lives, homes, businesses and emergency responders at risk,” the alert continued.
Phil Garrigan, chair of the National Fire Chiefs Council, said the number of wildfires seen this year had already surpassed all-time records.

“We’re only in the middle of August, and the wildfire season seems to extend way into November at this moment in time. So, we’re ⁠anticipating this being not just a record-breaking year, but a considerable increase on the number of wildfires previously experienced,” he told Reuters.
“We’ve declared 11 major incidents over the course of ⁠the last 24 hours,” Garrigan added.

“The demands and the requests for support have probably outstripped the capability of the U.K. fire and rescue service ... so we’ve struggled to ‌give fire and rescue services exactly ​what they want.”
Fires spread across Europe

Many European countries are battling fires after a long stretch of hot and dry conditions. A raging wildfire in the province of Huelva, southern Spain, triggered an operation to evacuate around ​700 people on Thursday.

More than 2,000 people evacuated ​the village of Gey in western Germany on Friday after a ‌wildfire near the Belgian border, while France evacuated 525 people from the village of Luglon in its southwestern Landes region.

Meanwhile, Croatia and Greece both evacuated tourists from resorts as fires spread. Flames enveloped settlements and trees around Omis, a scenic town on Croatia’s prized Dalmatian coast surrounded by trees and ⁠rocky hills, officials said, injuring 40 and forcing 1,200 to ​evacuate.
More than 300 people were evacuated by boat from Siviri in northern Greece, south of the country’s second city, Thessaloniki.

People wearing face masks, some clutching children or pets, boarded dinghies and boats in the seaside town as a wildfire ate through the nearby forest and columns of smoke turned the cloudless sky a dark gray.
